section_structure.heading: Introduction
section_structure.summary: Locates phantasia (φαντασία) within Aristotle's psychological treatises as one of the parts (μόρια) or faculties/powers (δυνάμεις) of the soul that cannot exist apart from sensation (αἴσθησις) and thought (διάνοια). Announces the three-stage methodological program: (I) brief presentation of Aristotle's concepts of the various parts/faculties of the soul and their correlation with classes of living beings; (II) outline of phantasia as (a) the faculty by which a phantasma is presented to us, (b) the faculty distinct from sensation, opinion, knowledge, intellect, and (c) the type of motion (κίνησις) generated by actual perception; with careful attention to the interpretation of φάντασμα in Aristotelian texts; (III) demonstration that Aristotle in DA III distinguishes three (not two) kinds or grades of phantasia. Cites Durrant's gloss on De Anima as 'the first systematic attempt to deal with a whole range of topics... falling under the general heading of Philosophical Psychology.'

section_structure.heading: I. Parts (Μόρια) or Faculties/Powers (Δυνάμεις) of the Soul
section_structure.summary: Hylomorphic foundation: soul as ἐντελέχεια ἡ πρώτη σώματος φυσικοῦ ὀργανικοῦ (DA II.1, 412b5-6) — soul as form (μορφή/εἶδος) of body, body as matter (ὕλη), one composite substance. Aristotle assigns parts/faculties of the soul corresponding to different kinds of living beings; these form a unified whole. DA III.9, 432a22-24: parts of the soul are 'in a sense innumerable.' Three-fold tripartition adduced via three texts: (a) De Gen. Anim. II.3 736b8-14 (nutritive/sensitive/rational); (b) DA II.4 415a14-18 and III.9 432b6-7 (nutritive/sensitive/rational); (c) Eth. Nic. I.7 1098a1-5 (nutritive-and-growth/perceptive/active-element-with-rational-principle). Papachristou then expands the threefold scheme: (1) nutritive (θρεπτική) = reproductive (γεννητική) — common to all living beings, plants and animals; functions better in sleep; (2) sensitive (αἰσθητική) — in all animals; does not exist apart from nutritive in plants; in actuality not potentiality; (3) rational (νοητικόν) or discursive (διανοητικόν) and intellect (νοῦς) — in humans. Philoponus' gloss: διανοητικόν = δυνάμει νοῦς (potential mind), analogous to passive mind (παθητικός νοῦς, 'becomes all things'); contrasted with ἐνεργείᾳ or ἐντελεχείᾳ νοῦς (= ποιητικός νοῦς, active mind). DA II.3 413b11-13 adds locomotive (κινητικόν κατὰ τόπον) — progressive motion (πορευτική κίνησις). DA II.3 414a31-32 adds appetitive (ὀρεκτικόν) — including desire (ἐπιθυμία), spiritedness (θυμός), wish (βούλησις); appetitive belongs to everything with sensation. DA III.9 432a28-432b4 adds imaginative (φανταστικόν), distinct from other parts but difficult to align with them. Concludes with Table 1: six-fold division — (1) Nutritive/Reproductive, (2) Appetitive, (3) Sensitive, (4) Locomotive, (5) Imaginative, (6) Rational/Discursive (Passive Mind) with Active Mind acting on Passive Mind.

section_structure.heading: II. Phantasia (Φαντασία) and Phantasma (Φάντασμα) in De Anima III.3
section_structure.summary: Phantasia as main subject of DA III.3. Definition at 428a1-2: εἰ δή ἐστιν ἡ φαντασία καθ' ἥν λέγομεν φάντασμά τι ἡμῖν γίγνεσθαι ('phantasia is the faculty/power by which a phantasma is presented to us'). Contrasts with the contemporary view that defines imagination as the capacity to recombine and call up mental images of objects not present to the senses. Aristotle's concept is wider — Ross's list: (a) after-images, (b) memory (μνήμη), (c) recollection (ἀνάμνησις), (d) dreams (ἐνύπνια), (e) in relation to desire (ἐπιθυμία), (f) in relation to thought (τὸ νοητικόν). Schofield: 'Aristotle gave the first extended analytical description of imagining as a distinct faculty of the soul.' Castoriadis dissent (fn. 35): Aristotle 'discovers' imagination philosophically but what he says thematically is of little consequence next to its hidden operation. DA I.1 403a8-10: 'if thinking is a kind of phantasia, then it would not be possible even for thinking to be independent of the body.' Phantasia differs from Plato's Sophist account ('mixture of sensation and judgement') because for Aristotle it is distinct from both αἴσθησις and διάνοια. Phantasia is a κίνησις in the soul caused by activity of sensation (DA III.3 428b11-13, 429a1-2). It involves ὑπόληψις (supposition), which includes knowledge, practical wisdom, opinion (per Philoponus). Phantasia is a πάθος (affection) in our own power (ἐφ' ἡμῖν), unlike judgement which is constrained by truth/falsity. Key passage on mnemonics: πρὸ ὀμμάτων γὰρ ἔστι τι ποιήσασθαι ('it is possible to set something before our eyes'), associated with mnemonic technique invented by Simonides of Ceos. Phantasia thus associated/identified with visual imagery — 'seeing with the mind's eye.' Translation of φάντασμα: (a) 'representation' or 'image' when related only to phantasia-faculty (e.g. 428a1-2); (b) 'mental representation' or 'mental image' when described as substratum upon which mind works (e.g. 431a16-17 διὸ οὐδέποτε νοεῖ ἄνευ φαντάσματος ἡ ψυχή).

section_structure.heading: III(a). Indefinite/Indeterminate Phantasia (Ἀόριστος Φαντασία)
section_structure.summary: Opens the central tripartition. DA III.11 433b31-434a5: 'We must also consider what produces movement in the imperfect animals (τὰ ἀτελῆ), which have no sense but touch, whether they have phantasia or not... How could they have phantasia? Or is it that as their movements are indefinite/indeterminate (ἀορίστως), they have phantasia... but indefinitely?' Three commentator-witnesses to indefinite phantasia: (i) Themistius, Libros Aristotelis de Anima Paraphrasis 5.3.122.11-12 — imperfect animals (τὰ ἀτελέστερα ζῷα) imagine indeterminately (ἀορίστως); they have phantasia ἀδιάρθρωτον (inarticulate) and συγκεχυμένην (confused); (ii) Philoponus, Aristotelis de Anima 15.592.26-29 — zoophytes (ζωοφύτοις, animals resembling plants such as corals, sea anemones, sponges, molluscs) have ἀορίστως phantasia because their movement is ἀόριστον (indeterminate); their movement contracts and expands more or less, indefinitely; (iii) AQUINAS, Sentencia libri De anima, Liber II (Corpus Thomisticum, ed. Busa SJ) at fn. 57: 'animalia imperfecta, ut in tertio dicetur, habent quidem phantasiam, sed indeterminatam, quia scilicet motus phantasiae non remanet in eis post apprehensionem sensus: in animalibus autem perfectis remanet motus phantasiae, etiam abeuntibus sensibilibus' ('imperfect animals... have phantasy, but it is one which is indeterminate because the motion of phantasy does not remain in them after the apprehension of the sense; however in perfect animals the motion of phantasy remains even after the sensible thing is gone'). Conclusion: imperfect/indefinite creatures with no sense except touch have indefinite phantasia; phantasmata of touch (tactile representations) are usually diffuse and indefinite and do not remain after the sense object is gone. Table 2 visualizes: Imperfect Animals (zoophytes, molluscs) → Only Contact Sense → Indefinite/Indeterminate Phantasia → tactile phantasmata diffuse, do not persist.

section_structure.heading: III(b). Sensitive Phantasia (Αἰσθητική Φαντασία)
section_structure.summary: Sensitive phantasia is generated by sense-perception (αἰσθάνεσθαι); does not occur without sense-perception; found in all animals other than man — namely the irrational animals (DA III.10 433b29-30; III.11 434a5-7). Excursus on desire (ἐπιθυμία) and animal movement: Ross identifies two kinds of desire — wish (βούλησις, rational, for future good) and appetite (ὄρεξις, irrational, for present pleasure-mistaken-for-good); Aristotle stresses appetite as cause of movement in animals (DA III.10 433b17-19). Critical thesis: ὀρεκτικὸν δὲ οὐκ ἄνευ φαντασίας ('the appetitive cannot exist without phantasia,' III.10 433b28-29). Aquinas (fn. 67, Kocourek trans.): 'the motion of phantasy does not remain in them [imperfect animals] after the apprehension of the sense.' The difference between indefinite and sensitive phantasia rests on capacity to perceive and retain a sense object: imperfect animals lack retention; normal animals with more than one sense (and thus capacity to discriminate distant objects) retain phantasmata after sense-object is gone. The ant-bee-scolex puzzle (DA III.3 428a8-11): Aristotle seems to deny phantasia to the ant, bee, and scolex (μύρμηξ, μέλιττα, σκώληξ). Hamlyn calls this 'puzzling' since 'doubtful Aristotle would have denied imagination to ants and bees.' Papachristou agrees with Hamlyn and rebuts via four texts: (a) Hist. Anim. I.1 488a7-10 — ants and bees are political animals (πολιτικά); (b) De Part. Anim. II.2 648a6-7 — bees are more intelligent (φρονιμώτερα) than many other animals; (c) Metaph. I.1 980b22-25 — bees are prudent/intelligent and have memory (μνήμη); (d) De Memoria I 450a12-17 — memory involves phantasia (οὐκ ἄνευ φαντάσματος). Forbes (1930): σκώληξ is not 'grub' but the first-stage larva or egg-like form of insect life. Papachristou accepts Torstrik's emendation 'δοκεῖ, οἷον μύρμηκι μὲν ἢ μελίττη, σκώληκι δ' οὔ' ('it seems that phantasia is found in the ant and the bee, but not in the scolex') — supported by Themistius and Sophonias, attested by Hicks, Wallace, Ross. Therefore ants and bees have sensitive phantasia; scolex (first-stage larva) does not. Table 3 visualizes: Irrational Animals → Senses of Taste/Touch/Smell/Sight/Hearing → Sensitive Phantasia → phantasmata of all five senses retained after object gone. Section closes with Table 4: Aristotle's Classification of Animals — Blooded/Vertebrates (Man, Viviparous Quadrupeds, Cetacea, Birds, Oviparous Quadrupeds/Footless Animals/Reptiles/Amphibians, Fishes) vs. Bloodless/Invertebrates (Hard-Shelled, Weak-Shelled, Cephalopoda, Insects, Zoophytes).

section_structure.heading: III(c). Calculative or Deliberative Phantasia (Λογιστική or Βουλευτική Φαντασία)
section_structure.summary: Third kind: calculative (λογιστική) or deliberative (βουλευτική). DA III.10 433b29: 'φαντασία δὲ πᾶσα ἢ λογιστικὴ ἢ αἰσθητική' ('all phantasia is either calculative or sensitive'). DA III.11 434a7: 'ἡ δὲ βουλευτικὴ [φαντασία] ἐν τοῖς λογιστικοῖς' ('the deliberative phantasia [exists] in the rational/calculating beings'). Note: λογιστική and βουλευτική are equivalent epithets; the verbs λογίζομαι and βουλεύομαι both mean 'to determine, consider.' DA III.11 434a5-12 (key passage): 'Sensitive phantasia exists in other animals; but deliberative phantasia [exists] only in those animals that can calculate; for whether one will do this or that is already a work of calculation; and there must be a single measure (μετρεῖν), for one pursues what is greater. Hence one has the ability to make one phantasma out of many phantasmata (δύναται ἓν ἐκ πλειόνων φαντασμάτων ποιεῖν).' Found only in animals possessing reason — Ross: 'deliberative imagination... is the monopoly of reasoning beings.' Rational beings do not always act according to plan (calculative phantasia); they can act according to awareness of the moment (sensitive phantasia). Aristotle's reason for denying opinion (δόξα) to non-human animals: their desires lack deliberation; only intellect-and-language-bearing beings have phantasia derived from inference (συλλογισμός). Calculative phantasia is intermediate between sense-perception (αἰσθάνεσθαι) and mind (νοῦς); involves having and combining several phantasmata into one — the elaboration, organization, unification of images typical of human beings. Calculative phantasia involves phantasmata with (a) propositional content (DA III.11 434a7-8: 'πότερον γὰρ πράξει τόδε ἢ τόδε') and (b) pictorial or quasi-pictorial content (DA III.7 431b6-8: 'τοῖς ἐν τῇ ψυχῇ φαντάσμασιν ἢ νοήμασιν ὥσπερ ὁρῶν λογίζεται καὶ βουλεύεται τὰ μέλλοντα πρὸς τὰ παρόντα' — 'and when by phantasmata or noêmata in the soul it calculates as if seeing them, and deliberates what is going to happen in the future in relation to the present'). Connection to modern cognitive science (fn. 94): the analog/pictorial vs. propositional representation debate (Kosslyn vs. Pylyshyn/Fodor) finds prefiguration in Aristotle's distinction. Table 5: Rational Animals → Senses + Sensitive Phantasia → Calculative or Deliberative Phantasia → mental images both pictorial/quasi-pictorial AND propositional, retained AND combined → Nous.

section_structure.heading: IV. Conclusion
section_structure.summary: Aristotle's treatment of phantasia is complicated. Phantasia is a faculty of the soul (φανταστικόν) placed between sensation (αἴσθησις) and thought (διάνοια). On one hand it depends on sensation, is a kind of affection (πάθος); on the other it is a necessary condition for memory, motion, desire, dreaming, thinking. Phantasmata are products of phantasia resulting from sense-perception (αἰσθάνεσθαι) — mental representations or mental images of sense objects with several functions (remembering, thinking). The conclusive thesis: a detailed study of DA III leads to the conclusion that Aristotle discriminates not two but THREE kinds or grades of phantasia: (a) indefinite/indeterminate phantasia (ἀόριστος φαντασία) in imperfectly developed creatures (zoophytes, molluscs) which have only the sense of touch — power of forming diffuse and indefinite phantasmata; (b) sensitive phantasia (αἰσθητική φαντασία) in animals possessing more than one sense — power of forming more vivid phantasmata; (c) calculative or deliberative phantasia (λογιστική or βουλευτική φαντασία) — the highest development of phantasia, only in humans, who can think and combine several mental images into one. Thomas J. T. Nigel: 'the impact on latter thinkers of Aristotle's account of cognition in general, and of imagery and imagination in particular, was enormous, and extended far beyond those who were avowed Aristotelians.' Aristotle's treatment exerts important influence on Hellenistic philosophy (Stoic theory of phantasia) and Western thought (Medieval — Aquinas — and Modern — Descartes' faculty of imagination). Concludes by pointing forward: deep conceptual relationship between Aristotle's theory of phantasia/phantasmata and the current mental-imagery/imagery debate — 'an issue that needs further investigation.'

outline: Cluster 1 (PDF 1, book 19, Title + Abstract): Papachristou announces her targeted intervention. Phantasia (φαντασία) is one of the parts (μόρια) or faculties/powers (δυνάμεις) of the soul that cannot exist apart from sensation (αἴσθησις) and thought (διάνοια). Its function and connection with phantasmata (φαντάσματα) plays a significant role in the psychological treatises of the Aristotelian Corpus. The paper's stated purpose: examine the concept of phantasia in De Anima III.3 and 'show that the Stageirite philosopher distinguishes THREE and NOT TWO kinds of phantasia, starting from the lowest, which is found in imperfect creatures, to the highest, which appears only in the human beings.' This is the signature thesis of the article — a corrective to the standard reading that finds only the λογιστική/αἰσθητική dichotomy at DA III.10 433b29.

Cluster 2 (PDF 1-2, book 19-20, Introduction): Reception-frame. Aristotle's De Anima (Περὶ Ψυχῆς) is characterized as Aristotle's psychology — most of the discussion deals with 'mental' functions though with admixture of physiology and biology. Durrant is quoted: De Anima is 'the first systematic attempt to deal with a whole range of topics... falling under the general heading of Philosophical Psychology.' The methodological plan is announced in three steps: (I) Aristotle's concepts of the parts/faculties of the soul and their correlation with classes of living beings; (II) phantasia as (a) faculty by which a phantasma is presented to us (DA III.3 428a1-2), (b) faculty distinct from sensation/opinion/knowledge/intellect, (c) a type of motion (κίνησις) generated by actual perception (DA III.3 429a1-2); careful interpretation of φάντασμα; (III) demonstration of the three-kinds thesis.

Cluster 3 (PDF 3-4, book 21-22, §I opening — Hylomorphism and Tripartite Soul): Soul as ἐντελέχεια ἡ πρώτη σώματος φυσικοῦ ὀργανικοῦ ('the first actuality of a natural organic body,' DA II.1 412b5-6). Hylomorphic relation: soul as μορφή/εἶδος of body, body as ὕλη of soul — one composite substance. The soul is inseparable from the body. Aristotle distinguishes parts/faculties of the soul corresponding to different kinds of living beings; these perform specific functions but form a unified whole. DA III.9 432a22-24 acknowledges an 'aporia' — in a sense parts of the soul are 'innumerable.' Three faculties emerge from three texts: De Gen. Anim. II.3 736b8-14 (nutritive/sensitive/rational); DA II.4 415a14-18 + III.9 432b6-7 (the τριμερής ψυχή formula); Eth. Nic. I.7 1098a1-5 (nutritive-growth/perceptive/active-element-with-rational-principle).

Cluster 4 (PDF 4-7, book 22-25, §I — Six-fold Expansion of Soul-Powers): Beyond the basic three, Papachristou marshals a six-fold scheme: (1) Nutritive (θρεπτική) = Reproductive (γεννητική) — common to all living beings (DA II.4 416a19-20), functions better in sleep (Eth. Eud. II.1 1219b22-23); (2) Sensitive (αἰσθητική) — in all animals, not in plants apart from nutritive; exists in actuality not potentiality (DA II.5 417a6-7); (3) Rational (νοητικόν) or Discursive (διανοητικόν) and Mind (νοῦς) — in humans (DA II.3 414b16-19). Philoponus' Aristotelis de Anima 15.255.4-5 glosses διανοητικόν as δυνάμει νοῦς ('potential mind'), analogous to παθητικός νοῦς ('passive mind, which becomes all things' — DA III.5 430a14-15) as distinct from ποιητικός νοῦς ('active mind'); Simplicius In De Anima 11.242.17-18 corroborates; Alexander of Aphrodisias De Anima 81.24-25 calls passive mind ὑλικός νοῦς ('mind like matter'). Papachristou's footnote 20 cross-references her dissertation (Thessaloniki 2008, Part 4 Ch. 3 pp. 273-300): she argues DA III.5 distinguishes not just two minds but that the duality of a single mind parallels the distinction between physical brain (matter contained in skull) and the 'energetic function of thought' — citing Ierodiakonou 2004 and her own 2008 article on the brain.

Cluster 5 (PDF 7-9, book 25-27, §I — Locomotive, Appetitive, Imaginative): DA II.2 413b11-13 adds the locomotive (κινητικόν κατὰ τόπον) — 'progressive motion' (πορευτική κίνησις, DA III.9 432b8-14). DA II.3 414a31-32 adds the appetitive (ὀρεκτικόν), including desire (ἐπιθυμία), spiritedness (θυμός), wish (βούλησις). Appetitive belongs to everything with sensation: cross-reference DA II.3 414b1-2; DA III.10 433a21 ('that which produces movement is one in kind, the appetitive faculty'); DA III.10 433b27-29 ('the animal is capable of movement itself so far as it is appetitive; and it cannot be appetitive without phantasia' — key for the tripartite scheme). Appetitive is both rational (βούλησις = wish) and irrational (ἐπιθυμία + θυμός = desire and spiritedness). DA III.9 432a28-432b4 adds the imaginative (φανταστικόν) — distinct from other parts but it is difficult to say with which of the parts it is identical. Table 1 summarizes: (1) Nutritive/Reproductive, (2) Appetitive (desire, spiritedness, wish), (3) Sensitive, (4) Locomotive, (5) Imaginative, (6a) Rational/Discursive → Passive Mind; (6b) Mind → Active Mind acting on Passive Mind.

Cluster 6 (PDF 10-11, book 28-29, §II opening — Phantasia and Phantasma): Phantasia is the main subject of DA III.3. Cited at the opening of the analysis: 'εἰ δή ἐστιν ἡ φαντασία καθ' ἥν λέγομεν φάντασμά τι ἡμῖν γίγνεσθαι' (DA III.3 428a1-2) — 'phantasia is the faculty/power by which a phantasma is presented to us.' Papachristou's translation-policy: she prefers to leave the Greek word untranslated rather than render it 'imagination,' on the grounds that 'imagination' does not convey Aristotle's notion 'as honestly and as understandably as possible' (fn. 32). The contemporary view defines imagination as the capacity to create/recombine/reproduce/call-up mental images of objects not present to the senses. Aristotle's wider concept is laid out via Ross's six-function list: (a) formation of after-images, (b) memory (μνήμη), (c) recollection (ἀνάμνησις), (d) dreams (ἐνύπνια), (e) in relation to desire (ἐπιθυμία), (f) in relation to thought (τὸ νοητικόν). Schofield (1978): 'it was Aristotle who gave the first extended analytical description of imagining as a distinct faculty of the soul' — the imaginative part (τὸ φανταστικὸν μόριον), which cannot be independent of the body (DA I.1 403a8-10). Castoriadis dissents (fn. 35): Aristotle 'discovers' imagination philosophically but what he says about it thematically — 'fixing the imagination in its alleged place, between sensation and intellection, of which it would be a reproduction, and intellection' — is of little consequence next to what he has truly to say about it, which he has 'no way of reconciling with what he thinks about phusis, the soul, thinking and being.' Papachristou cites Castoriadis but does not endorse the dissent.

Cluster 7 (PDF 11-13, book 29-31, §II — Phantasia distinct from Sensation, Thought, Plato's Sophist): Aristotle differentiates phantasia from sensation (αἴσθησις) and thought (διάνοια) at DA III.3 427b14-15. The differentiation entails that Aristotle's phantasia diverges from Plato's Sophist account where phantasia is described as a 'mixture of sensation and judgement' (σύμμειξις αἰσθήσεως καὶ δόξης, Plato Sophist 264a4-b3). For Aristotle phantasia is a kind of motion (κίνησις) in the soul that cannot exist apart from sensation — it is caused by the activity of sensation (DA III.3 428b11-13: 'ἡ δὲ φαντασία κίνησίς τις δοκεῖ εἶναι καὶ οὐκ ἄνευ αἰσθήσεως γίγνεσθαι ἀλλ' αἰσθανομένοις καὶ ὧν αἴσθησίς ἐστιν'; III.3 429a1-2). It also involves ὑπόληψις (supposition) — a term that Philoponus glosses as inclusive of knowledge (ἐπιστήμη), practical wisdom (φρόνησις), and opinion (δόξα). Hamlyn calls ὑπόληψις 'a difficult word to translate since it appears to express a very general notion which functions somewhat as the notion of judgement did in the writings of the Absolute Idealists'; Hamlyn-Polansky and Hicks render it 'supposition.' Caujolle-Zaslawsky (1996) is cited in fn. 45 as further discussion. Phantasia is a πάθος (affection) that is in our own power (ἐφ' ἡμῖν) — 'it is up to us to imagine, but it is not up to us to believe, for the belief that we hold must be either false or true' (DA III.3 427b14-21).

Cluster 8 (PDF 13-14, book 31-32, §II — Mnemonics and Visual Imagery): The phrase 'πρὸ ὀμμάτων γὰρ ἔστι τι ποιήσασθαι' (DA III.3 427b18-19) — 'for it is possible to set something before our eyes' — is given pride of place. It means our ability to voluntarily (ὅταν βουλώμεθα) set mental images before our eyes, as do those who use memorization techniques based on sight and the powers of visualization (οἱ ἐν τοῖς μνημονικοῖς τιθέμενοι καὶ εἰδωλοποιοῦντες). Papachristou identifies these as Mnemonics — the mnemonic art invented by the Greek lyric poet Simonides of Ceos (556-469 B.C.). Phantasia thus seems to be associated or even identified with VISUAL IMAGERY — 'the ability to form mental images, or to ‘see with the mind’s eye.’' Example: if asked to describe a lion not physically present, we find ourselves 'looking at' or 'visualizing' lions with ‘our mind’s eye.’ Vasileios Tatakis (fn. 49) translates πρὸ ὀμμάτων as 'for it is possible to represent an object before the soul's eye' — justified by Eth. Nic. VI.13 1144a29-30. NB Aristotle's note in DA I 459a15-23 (De Insomniis): dream images (ἐνύπνια) formed while asleep, which we cannot voluntarily produce, count as products of phantasia even though perception and judgement are absent in sleep.

Cluster 9 (PDF 14-15, book 32-33, §II closing — Translating Φάντασμα): Papachristou's translation policy for φάντασμα. The word appears twelve times in DA: 428a1, 431a14-17, 431a16-17 (διὸ οὐδέποτε νοεῖ ἄνευ φαντάσματος ἡ ψυχή), 431b2-8, 432a8-14, 434a9-10. Two registers: (a) 'representation' or 'image' when φάντασμα is related only to the phantasia faculty (as at 428a1-2); (b) 'mental representation' or 'mental image' when φάντασμα is described by the philosopher as the substratum upon which the mind works (as at 431a16-17). This distinction will matter for the tripartite scheme.

Cluster 10 (PDF 15-17, book 33-35, §III(a) — Indefinite/Indeterminate Phantasia): Opens the three-kinds discussion. DA III.11 433b31-434a5: 'Σκεπτέον δὲ καὶ περὶ τῶν ἀτελῶν, τί τὸ κινοῦν ἐστιν, οἷς ἀφῇ μόνον ὑπάρχει αἴσθησις, πότερον ἐνδέχεται φαντασίαν ὑπάρχειν τούτοις, ἢ οὔ;...φαντασία δὲ πῶς ἂν ἐνείη; ἢ ὥσπερ καὶ κινεῖται ἀορίστως, καὶ ταῦτ' ἔνεστι μέν, ἀορίστως δ' ἔνεστιν' ('We must also consider what produces movement in the imperfect animals, which have no sense but touch, whether they have phantasia or not... How could they have phantasia? Or is it that as their movements are indefinite/indeterminate, they have phantasia... but indefinitely?'). Three commentator-witnesses follow.

Cluster 11 (PDF 16, book 34, §III(a) — Themistius and Philoponus): Themistius' Libros Aristotelis de Anima Paraphrasis 5.3.122.11-12: 'φαντάζεται ἀορίστως, ὥστε ἔχει μὲν φαντασίαν, ἀδιάρθωτον δὲ καὶ συγκεχυμένην' — imperfect animals (τὰ ἀτελέστερα ζῷα), the lowest forms of animals, imagine indeterminately and so have phantasia, but in an inarticulate (ἀδιάρθωτον) and confused (συγκεχυμένην) way. Philoponus' Aristotelis de Anima 15.592.26-29: zoophytes (ζωοφύτοις — animals resembling plants, such as corals, sea anemones, sponges, molluscs) have ἀορίστως phantasia because the movement of these creatures is ἀόριστον (indeterminate); their movement contracts and expands more or less, indefinitely.

Cluster 12 (PDF 16-17, book 34-35, §III(a) — Aquinas's Latin Witness): Thomas Aquinas explains that imperfect animals (animalia imperfecta) possess an indeterminate phantasia (phantasia indeterminata). This phantasia is indeterminate because the motion of phantasia (motus phantasiae) does not remain in this kind of creatures after the sense object is gone. Quotation from Sentencia libri De anima Liber II (Corpus Thomisticum, ed. Roberto Busa SJ, Taurini 1959): 'Videtur tamen hoc esse contrarium ei quod supra dixerat: quia si pars decisa habet sensum et appetitum, habet etiam phantasiam; si tamen phantasia est idem cum imaginatione, ut videtur. Dicendum est igitur, quod animalia imperfecta, ut in tertio dicetur, habent quidem phantasiam, sed indeterminatam, quia scilicet motus phantasiae non remanet in eis post apprehensionem sensus: in animalibus autem perfectis remanet motus phantasiae, etiam abeuntibus sensibilibus. Et secundum hoc, dicitur hic quod imaginatio non est eadem omnibus animalibus. Sed quaedam animalia sunt, quae hac sola vivunt, carentia scilicet intellectu, et directa in suis operationibus per imaginationem, sicut nos dirigimur per intellectum.' English (Kocourek translation, fn. 57): 'Nevertheless, this seems to be contrary to what he said above: because if a part cut off has sense and appetite, it also has phantasy; provided that phantasy is the same as imagination, as it seems. It must be said, therefore, that imperfect animals, as is said in the third book, do really have phantasy, but it is one which is indeterminate because the motion of phantasy does not remain in them after the apprehension of the sense; however in perfect animals the motion of phantasy remains even after the sensible thing is gone. And according to this it is said here that imagination is not the same for all animals. But there are certain animals which live by this alone, lacking the intellect and being directed in their operations by imagination, just as we are directed by the intellect.' Papachristou's gloss: imperfect/indefinite creatures have no sense except that of touch (the contact sense, ἀφή — Polansky notes the word at 434a1 may apply to both touch and taste); they possess an indefinite/indeterminate kind of phantasia; representations of touch (phantasmata) or tactile representations are usually diffuse and indefinite and do not remain in them after the sense object is gone. Table 2 visualizes the scheme.

Cluster 13 (PDF 17-19, book 35-37, §III(b) — Sensitive Phantasia, Desire, Appetite): Next kind. Aristotle says sensitive phantasia is generated by sense-perception (αἰσθάνεσθαι); does not occur without sense-perception; found in all animals other than man (DA III.10 433b29-30: 'ταύτης μὲν οὖν καὶ τὰ ἄλλα ζῷα μετέχει'; III.11 434a5-7: 'ἡ μὲν οὖν αἰσθητικὴ φαντασία, ὥσπερ εἴρηται, καὶ ἐν τοῖς ἄλλοις ζῴοις ὑπάρχει'). Sets up question: if sensitive phantasia is shared by all animals — even imperfect ones — what is the difference between indefinite and sensitive phantasia? Excursus on desire and animal movement: David Ross identifies two kinds of desire — wish (βούλησις, rational, for future good) and appetite (ὄρεξις/ἐπιθυμία, irrational, for present pleasure-mistaken-for-good). Aristotle stresses appetite as cause of animal movement: DA III.10 433b17-19 ('κινεῖται γὰρ τὸ κινούμενον ᾗ ὀρέγεται, καὶ ἡ ὄρεξις κίνησίς τίς ἐστιν ἢ ἐνέργεια'). Crucial: 'ὀρεκτικὸν δὲ οὐκ ἄνευ φαντασίας' (DA III.10 433b28-29) — the appetitive cannot exist without phantasia; appetite moves the animal only with the mediation of phantasia.

Cluster 14 (PDF 19-20, book 37-38, §III(b) — The Distinction Resolved): The Aquinas-driven solution to the indefinite/sensitive distinction. Aquinas (in St. Thomas Aquinas, The Commentary of St. Thomas Aquinas on Aristotle's Treatise On the Soul, trans. R. A. Kocourek, College of St. Thomas 1946, p. 19, fn. 67): 'the motion of phantasy does not remain in them after the apprehension of the sense' — said of imperfect animals. In animals other than indefinite creatures — in normal animals that possess more than one sense and so can discriminate distant objects — the product of phantasia or phantasma REMAINS in them even after the sense object is gone. The difference between the indefinite and sensitive kinds of phantasia is grounded in their capacity to PERCEIVE and RETAIN a sense object. Very slight traces of sensitive phantasia are found in indefinite animals (they can discriminate pleasant/unpleasant on contact), but cannot sense at a distance. Table 3 visualizes: Irrational Animals → Senses of Taste/Touch/Smell/Sight/Hearing (objects in contact AND at distance) → Sensitive Phantasia → phantasmata retained after sense object gone.

Cluster 15 (PDF 20-22, book 38-40, §III(b) — The Ant, Bee, and Scolex Puzzle): The famous interpretive crux at DA III.3 428a8-11: 'εἶτα αἴσθησις μὲν ἀεὶ πάρεστι, φαντασία δ' οὔ. εἰ δὲ τῇ ἐνεργείᾳ τὸ αὐτό, πᾶσιν ἂν ἐνδέχοιτο τοῖς θηρίοις φαντασίαν ὑπάρχειν· δοκεῖ δ' οὔ, οἷον μύρμηκι ἢ μελίττῃ ἢ σκώληκι' — 'sense is always present, but not phantasia. But if [phantasia] was the same in actuality [with sense], it would be possible for all beasts to have phantasia; but it seems not to be the case; as the ant, the bee, and the scolex.' Hamlyn calls the passage 'puzzling since it is doubtful whether Aristotle would have denied imagination to ants and bees.' Papachristou agrees with Hamlyn. Four counter-textual witnesses are marshaled: (a) Hist. Anim. I.1 488a7-10 — Aristotle includes ants and bees among the POLITICAL animals (πολιτικά: man, the bee, the wasp, the ant, the crane); (b) De Part. Anim. II.2 648a6-7 — bees and similar animals are more intelligent (φρονιμώτερα) than many other animals; (c) Metaph. I.1 980b22-25 — bees are prudent/intelligent and have memory (μνήμη): 'and on this account these are more intelligent and apt at learning than those which cannot remember'; (d) De Mem. I 450a12-17 — memory involves phantasia: 'μνήμη... οὐκ ἄνευ φαντάσματός ἐστιν' ('memory is not without a phantasma'). William Forbes (Classical Philology 1930) on the σκώληξ: it 'has to be the first stage of the life-history of an insect or other creature which he [Aristotle] did not recognize as produced by birth or hatching from a real egg' — corresponds to the earthworm or maggot-like larvae of wasps (Hist. Anim. I.5 489b9-11; De Gen. Anim. II.1 733a1-2). Papachristou accepts Torstrik's emendation of DA 428a10-11: 'δοκεῖ, οἷον μύρμηκι μὲν ἢ μελίττη ἢ σκώληκι' → 'δοκεῖ, οἷον μύρμηκι μὲν ἢ μελίττη, σκώληκι δ' οὔ' ('it seems that phantasia is found in the ant and the bee, but NOT in the scolex'). Torstrik's emendation is supported by readings in Themistius (5.3.90.5-8) and Sophonias (55.27-32) and attested by Hicks 1907, Wallace 1976, Ross 1961. Conclusion: ants and bees, being intelligent creatures with memory, should be included among animals possessing sensitive phantasia. The scolex (first-stage larva or egg-form) does not have phantasia.

Cluster 16 (PDF 22, book 40, §III(b) — Aristotle's Classification of Animals): Table 4 visualizes the full Aristotelian zoology underwriting the tripartite scheme. Blooded/Vertebrates (Ἔναιμα — Hist. Anim. II.15 505b28-32: 'ἄνθρωπός τε καὶ τὰ ζῳοτόκα τῶν τετραπόδων, ἔτι δὲ καὶ τὰ ᾠοτόκα τῶν τετραπόδων καὶ ὄρνις καὶ ἰχθὺς καὶ κῆτος'): (1) Man, (2) Viviparous Quadrupeds, (3) Cetacea (whales, dolphins, seals), (4) Birds, (5) Oviparous Quadrupeds + Footless Animals (reptiles + amphibians), (6) Fishes. Bloodless/Invertebrates (Ἄναιμα — De Part. Anim. IV.5 678a27-31): (1) Hard-Shelled Animals (clams, oysters), (2) Weak-Shelled Animals (crabs), (3) Cephalopoda (squids, cuttle-fishes), (4) Insects, (5) Zoophytes (anemones, holothuria, sponges). The zoophytes and molluscs of the bloodless column populate the 'imperfect animals' tier; the ant and the bee belong to insects; all the rest of the irrational animals (including most of the vertebrates) have sensitive phantasia; man alone has the third kind.

Cluster 17 (PDF 23-24, book 41-42, §III(c) — Calculative or Deliberative Phantasia): Third kind. DA III.10 433b29: 'φαντασία δὲ πᾶσα ἢ λογιστικὴ ἢ αἰσθητική' — 'all phantasia is either calculative or sensitive.' This single sentence has been read as Aristotle's BINARY taxonomy. Papachristou's tripartite reading adds the indefinite tier underneath. DA III.11 434a7: 'ἡ δὲ βουλευτικὴ [φαντασία] ἐν τοῖς λογιστικοῖς' — 'the deliberative phantasia exists in the rational/calculating beings.' Methodological note: the epithets λογιστική (calculative) and βουλευτική (deliberative) are EQUIVALENT — the verbs λογίζομαι and βουλεύομαι both mean 'to determine, consider' (cf. Papatheodorou, Athens 'Papyrus' Publications). Andreas Papatheodorou (fn. 89): pleasure, interest, and duty are some of the standards or criteria of measurement that intelligent animals use to pursue what is superior. DA III.11 434a5-12 (the key passage): 'ἡ μὲν οὖν αἰσθητικὴ φαντασία, ὥσπερ εἴρηται, καὶ ἐν τοῖς ἄλλοις ζῴοις ὑπάρχει, ἡ δὲ βουλευτικὴ ἐν τοῖς λογιστικοῖς (πότερον γὰρ πράξει τόδε ἢ τόδε, λογισμοῦ ἤδη ἐστὶν ἔργον· καὶ ἀνάγκη ἑνὶ μετρεῖν· τὸ μεῖζον γὰρ διώκει. ὥστε δύναται ἓν ἐκ πλειόνων φαντασμάτων ποιεῖν)' — 'Sensitive phantasia exists in other animals; but deliberative phantasia exists in those animals that can calculate; for whether one will do this or that is already a work of calculation; and there must be a single measure (μετρεῖν), for one pursues what is greater. Hence one has the ability to MAKE ONE PHANTASMA OUT OF MANY PHANTASMATA.'

Cluster 18 (PDF 24-25, book 42-43, §III(c) — Calculative Phantasia and Intellect): The third kind is found only in animals that possess reason — Ross: 'the deliberative imagination, the rational imagination... is monopoly of reasoning beings, i.e. of men.' Rational beings do not always act according to plan (calculative phantasia); they can act according to awareness of the moment (sensitive phantasia). Aristotle's reason for denying opinion (δόξα) to non-human animals: their desires lack deliberation; only animals with intellect — and therefore language — have phantasia that comes from inference (συλλογισμός). Calculative phantasia is intermediate between αἰσθάνεσθαι (sense-perception) and νοῦς (mind). It involves having and combining several phantasmata into one. The elaboration, organization, and unification of phantasmata are typical characteristics of human beings. Table 5 visualizes: Rational Animals → Senses → Sensitive Phantasia → Calculative or Deliberative Phantasia → mental images both PICTORIAL/QUASI-PICTORIAL and PROPOSITIONAL, retained AND combined → Nous.

Cluster 19 (PDF 25, book 43, §III(c) — Propositional vs. Pictorial Content): The activity of calculative or deliberative phantasia involves phantasmata with (a) PROPOSITIONAL content — DA III.11 434a7-8: 'ἡ δὲ βουλευτικὴ ἐν τοῖς λογιστικοῖς (πότερον γὰρ πράξει τόδε ἢ τόδε, λογισμοῦ ἤδη ἐστὶν ἔργον)' — propositional choice between 'this or that' is the work of calculation; (b) PICTORIAL or QUASI-PICTORIAL content — DA III.7 431b6-8: 'ὅτε δὲ τοῖς ἐν τῇ ψυχῇ φαντάσμασιν ἢ νοήμασιν ὥσπερ ὁρῶν λογίζεται καὶ βουλεύεται τὰ μέλλοντα πρὸς τὰ παρόντα' — 'and when by phantasmata or noêmata in the soul it calculates as if seeing them, and deliberates what is going to happen in the future in relation to the present.' These two Aristotelian remarks are 'excellent... with respect to contemporary ideas about mental images.' Footnote 94 announces the contemporary cognitive-science bridge: the Analog/Pictorial Representation Account (Kosslyn, Sheppard) holds that visual information is stored in the brain in an analog or picture-like (quasi-pictorial) code; the Propositional Representation Account (Pylyshyn, Fodor) holds that visual information is stored in a propositional or word-like code. Aristotle's two passages map onto BOTH sides of the contemporary debate — calculative phantasia uses both kinds.

Cluster 20 (PDF 26-27, book 44-45, Conclusion): Aristotle's treatment of phantasia is a complicated subject. Phantasia is a faculty of the soul, the φανταστικόν, that is placed between sensation (αἴσθησις) and thought (διάνοια). On one hand it depends on sensation, is a kind of affection (πάθος); on the other it is a necessary condition for memory, motion, desire, dreaming, thinking — connected with a wide variety of psychological phenomena. Phantasmata are products of the function of phantasia, resulting from sense-perception (αἰσθάνεσθαι) — mental representations or mental images of sense objects, with several functions (remembering, thinking). The article's thesis is then restated: a detailed study of phantasia in DA Book III leads to the conclusion that the Stageirite philosopher discriminates not two — as is commonly argued — but THREE kinds or grades of phantasia: (a) indefinite/indeterminate phantasia (ἀόριστος φαντασία) in imperfectly developed creatures (zoophytes, molluscs) which have no sense except that of touch — power of formatting diffuse and indefinite phantasmata; (b) sensitive phantasia (αἰσθητική φαντασία) in animals that possess more than one sense (normal animals) — power of forming more vivid phantasmata; (c) calculative or deliberative phantasia (λογιστική or βουλευτική φαντασία) in human beings — the highest development of the faculty, who have the power of thinking and the ability to combine several mental images (phantasmata) into one.

Cluster 21 (PDF 27, book 45, Conclusion coda — Reception and Future Directions): Thomas J. T. Nigel (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 2013): 'the impact on latter thinkers of Aristotle's account of cognition in general, and of imagery and imagination in particular, was enormous, and extended far beyond those who were avowed Aristotelians.' Aristotle's treatment of phantasia in De Anima exerted important influence on (a) Hellenistic philosophy — the STOIC theory of phantasia (cf. fn. 96 and Papachristou's 2009 essay on Aristotelian phantasia in Stoic philosophy and Romanes); (b) Western thought, Medieval (St. Thomas Aquinas's account of imagination, imaginatio) and Modern (Descartes' views on the function of the faculty of imagination). Papachristou closes by pointing forward to a deeper conceptual relationship between Aristotle's theory and the current debate over mental images/mental imagery — 'another issue that needs further investigation.' Footnote 98 cross-references her own 2006 essay 'The Mental Images (Phantasmata) in Aristotle's De Anima and in S. Kosslyn's Contemporary Work' (in Demetra Sfendoni-Mentzou ed., The Aristotelian Philosophy and the Contemporary Scientific Thought, Aristotle University of Thessaloniki 2006, pp. 112-134).

concepts.label: tripartite phantasia scheme
concepts.gloss: Papachristou's signature thesis: Aristotle in DA III distinguishes THREE kinds or grades of phantasia (indefinite, sensitive, calculative/deliberative), not the binary λογιστική/αἰσθητική pair commonly read off DA III.10 433b29

concepts.label: phantasia indeterminata (Latin) / ἀόριστος φαντασία (Greek)
concepts.gloss: Indeterminate phantasia — the lowest grade; found in imperfect animals (animalia imperfecta / τὰ ἀτελῆ); phantasmata do not persist after the sense object is gone

concepts.label: motus phantasiae (Latin) / motion of phantasia
concepts.gloss: Aquinas's term (Sentencia libri De anima, Liber II) for the persistence — or non-persistence — of phantasia-motion after sense apprehension; the criterion separating animalia imperfecta from animalia perfecta

concepts.label: animalia imperfecta vs. animalia perfecta
concepts.gloss: Aquinas's Latin distinction (= τὰ ἀτελῆ vs. τέλεια ζῷα) for imperfect vs. perfect animals — the foundational zoological pairing for the tripartite scheme; imperfect = zoophytes, molluscs with only touch; perfect = animals with multiple senses retaining phantasmata

concepts.label: phantasia αἰσθητική (sensitive phantasia)
concepts.gloss: Second kind/middle tier — found in all animals other than man (irrational animals with multiple senses); generated by αἰσθάνεσθαι; retains phantasmata after sense object gone

concepts.label: phantasia λογιστική / βουλευτική (calculative / deliberative phantasia)
concepts.gloss: Third/highest kind — only in humans; involves combining many phantasmata into one (ἓν ἐκ πλειόνων φαντασμάτων ποιεῖν, DA III.11 434a10-11); the epithets are equivalent (λογίζομαι and βουλεύομαι both = 'to determine, consider')

concepts.label: phantasia as κίνησις ὑπὸ τῆς αἰσθήσεως κατ' ἐνέργειαν γιγνομένη
concepts.gloss: Aristotle's definition (DA III.3 428b11-13, 429a1-2): phantasia as a kind of motion in the soul caused by actual sense-perception

concepts.label: kath' hen formula for phantasia
concepts.gloss: DA III.3 428a1-2: phantasia is 'the faculty/power by which (καθ' ἥν) we say a phantasma is presented to us'

concepts.label: πρὸ ὀμμάτων ποιήσασθαι (setting before our eyes)
concepts.gloss: DA III.3 427b18-19: the mnemonist's ability voluntarily (ὅταν βουλώμεθα) to set images before our eyes; basis for Papachristou's reading of phantasia as VISUAL IMAGERY / 'seeing with the mind's eye'

concepts.label: ὑπόληψις (supposition)
concepts.gloss: Difficult term: Philoponus' gloss includes knowledge (ἐπιστήμη), practical wisdom (φρόνησις), and opinion (δόξα); Hamlyn calls it a difficulty similar to 'judgement' in Absolute Idealist usage; Hamlyn-Polansky and Hicks translate as 'supposition'

concepts.label: φάντασμα with two registers
concepts.gloss: Papachristou's translation policy: (a) 'representation/image' when φάντασμα relates only to phantasia (e.g. 428a1-2); (b) 'mental representation/mental image' when φάντασμα is substratum on which mind works (e.g. 431a16-17 διὸ οὐδέποτε νοεῖ ἄνευ φαντάσματος ἡ ψυχή)

concepts.label: ant-bee-scolex puzzle
concepts.gloss: DA III.3 428a8-11 seems to deny phantasia to ants, bees, scolex; Papachristou accepts Torstrik's emendation 'δοκεῖ, οἷον μύρμηκι μὲν ἢ μελίττη, σκώληκι δ' οὔ' — ants and bees have phantasia (sensitive), scolex does not

concepts.label: ἀδιάρθωτον καὶ συγκεχυμένη phantasia
concepts.gloss: Themistius' gloss (5.3.122.11-12): the inarticulate and confused character of indefinite/indeterminate phantasia in imperfect animals

concepts.label: zoophytes (ζωόφυτα) as imperfect-animal exemplars
concepts.gloss: Animals resembling plants — corals, sea anemones, sponges, molluscs; Philoponus' citation as exemplars of indefinite-phantasia bearers

concepts.label: appetite cannot exist without phantasia (ὀρεκτικὸν δὲ οὐκ ἄνευ φαντασίας)
concepts.gloss: DA III.10 433b28-29: appetite (cause of animal movement) requires phantasia mediation — the link between sensitive phantasia and animal locomotion

concepts.label: ἓν ἐκ πλειόνων φαντασμάτων ποιεῖν (making one phantasma out of many)
concepts.gloss: DA III.11 434a10-11: the signature mark of calculative/deliberative phantasia — the unification of multiple phantasmata; what distinguishes rational from sensitive phantasia

concepts.label: propositional vs. pictorial phantasmata
concepts.gloss: Papachristou's distinctive analytic move: calculative phantasia uses phantasmata with BOTH propositional content (DA III.11 434a7-8: 'πότερον... τόδε ἢ τόδε') AND pictorial/quasi-pictorial content (DA III.7 431b6-8: 'ὥσπερ ὁρῶν λογίζεται'). Maps onto contemporary Kosslyn-vs-Pylyshyn debate

concepts.label: blooded/bloodless animal classification
concepts.gloss: Aristotle's Hist. Anim. II.15 505b28-32 and De Part. Anim. IV.5 678a27-31 dichotomy (Ἔναιμα/Ἄναιμα = Vertebrates/Invertebrates); Table 4 of the article

concepts.label: soul as ἐντελέχεια ἡ πρώτη σώματος φυσικοῦ ὀργανικοῦ

concepts.label: six-fold division of soul-powers

readings.label: Tripartite-not-binary thesis: three kinds of phantasia in DA III
readings.thesis: Against the standard reading that finds only two kinds of phantasia in Aristotle (λογιστική/αἰσθητική at DA III.10 433b29), Papachristou argues that DA III.11 433b31-434a5 — together with the testimony of Themistius, Philoponus, and Aquinas — establishes a THIRD, sub-sensitive kind: indefinite/indeterminate phantasia (ἀόριστος φαντασία / phantasia indeterminata) found in imperfect animals (zoophytes, molluscs) with only the contact sense. The three kinds correlate with three classes of animals: imperfect, irrational-perfect, rational.
readings.contestation: Directly extends/corrects the conventional taxonomy assumed in Nussbaum (1985), Frede (1992), Caston (1995), Wedin (1988), Modrak (1986), and the Anglophone analytic tradition. The binary reading is not refuted as wrong; rather, the binary is shown to be incomplete — Aristotle's discussion of the imperfect animals at DA III.11 433b31-434a5 is read as evidence for a lower indefinite tier that the binary scheme cannot accommodate.

readings.label: Thomistic-philological method: Aquinas as authoritative interpretive frame
readings.thesis: The decisive move legitimating the tripartite reading is the citation of Aquinas's Sentencia libri De anima, Liber II at fn. 57 (Corpus Thomisticum, ed. Busa SJ): Aquinas's Latin distinction phantasia indeterminata / motus phantasiae / animalia imperfecta vs. perfecta gives the explicit conceptual machinery for separating an indefinite-phantasia tier from the sensitive tier. Papachristou treats Aquinas not as one commentator among others but as the privileged systematizer who makes the third kind visible. This is the Thomistic-reception backbone of the entire essay.
readings.contestation: This Thomistic anchoring distinguishes Papachristou's reading from the predominantly philological-Greek (Themistius, Philoponus) and Anglophone analytic readings. It places her in disciplinary kinship with WHITE 1985 (Thomistic sensibility, though Aquinas not named) and Phillipe 1971 (Thomist) and against the Wittgensteinian-Nussbaumian and the Schofield-Frede-Caston Anglophone tradition. The Thomistic frame is methodologically load-bearing — without it the tripartite reading lacks its strongest textus receptus.

readings.label: Retention-of-phantasmata as the criterion separating indefinite from sensitive phantasia
readings.thesis: The PHILOSOPHICAL difference between indefinite and sensitive phantasia is grounded in capacity to PERCEIVE and RETAIN a sense object. In imperfect animals (only touch), the motus phantasiae does not remain after the sense apprehension; in perfect/normal animals (multiple senses, can sense at a distance), the phantasma remains after the sense object is gone. This is Aquinas's criterion, used by Papachristou as the operative distinction.
readings.contestation: Maps onto Frede 1992's supervenience reading of phantasia on sensation: in Papachristou's terms, indefinite phantasia is barely-supervenient (slight traces) while sensitive phantasia is fully retentive. The temporal/retention criterion connects Papachristou's reading to White 1985's temporal-mediation thesis (phantasia 'lends to the appearances a stability') and to the broader Aristotelian doctrine of phantasia-as-storehouse of sensible forms freed from matter.

readings.label: Torstrik emendation: ants/bees do, scolex does not
readings.thesis: Reading DA III.3 428a8-11 with Torstrik's emendation (supported by Themistius and Sophonias and accepted by Hicks 1907, Wallace 1976, Ross 1961), the apparent denial of phantasia to ants, bees, and scolex is resolved: ants and bees possess phantasia (sensitive), but the scolex (first-stage larva, per Forbes 1930) does not. The four cross-textual witnesses are: ants and bees as political animals (Hist. Anim. I.1 488a7-10), more intelligent than many animals (De Part. Anim. II.2 648a6-7), prudent and memory-bearing (Metaph. I.1 980b22-25), and memory involves phantasia (De Mem. I 450a12-17).
readings.contestation: Aligns with Hamlyn's instinct that Aristotle cannot have denied phantasia to ants and bees; against the standard reading that takes 428a8-11 at face value. The emendation is essential for the tripartite scheme to function: without it, the boundary between sensitive and indefinite phantasia falls at the wrong place. Connects to Frede 1992 and Caston 1995's accounts of the cognitive sophistication of irrational animals.

readings.label: Propositional + pictorial dual-register of calculative phantasmata
readings.thesis: Calculative/deliberative phantasia uses phantasmata with BOTH propositional content (DA III.11 434a7-8: 'πότερον... τόδε ἢ τόδε') AND pictorial/quasi-pictorial content (DA III.7 431b6-8: 'ὥσπερ ὁρῶν λογίζεται'). The two Aristotelian remarks prefigure both sides of the contemporary cognitive-science debate over mental imagery — Kosslyn's analog/pictorial account and Pylyshyn/Fodor's propositional account.
readings.contestation: Distinctively interdisciplinary: imports the imagery debate (Kosslyn 1978 'Visual Images Preserve Metric Spatial Information,' Pylyshyn 1981 'The Imagery Debate,' Block 1981 Imagery) into the exegesis. No analogue in White 1985 (closed cosmos), Nussbaum 1985 (analytic-Wittgensteinian, no Kosslyn), Frede 1992 (no cognitive-science). Papachristou's own 2006 paper on phantasmata and Kosslyn provides the prior context.

readings.label: πρὸ ὀμμάτων ποιήσασθαι: phantasia as voluntary visual imagery
readings.thesis: DA III.3 427b18-19's clause 'it is possible to set something before our eyes' (πρὸ ὀμμάτων... ποιήσασθαι), said of those using mnemonic techniques (μνημονικοῖς τιθέμενοι), allows Papachristou to identify phantasia primarily with VISUAL IMAGERY — the ability to 'see with the mind's eye' voluntarily (ὅταν βουλώμεθα). The mnemonic art is attributed to Simonides of Ceos.
readings.contestation: The visual-imagery reading is in dialogue with the rhetorical-tradition phantasia (Gonzalez 2006 PHX-06, O'Gorman 2005 PHX-05, Hawhee 2011 PHX-07) — though Papachristou does not engage the rhetorical literature. Compatible with White 1985's lexical-genealogical analysis (phantasia from phaos = light) but pushes further into mnemonic-imagery territory.

readings.label: Cognitive-developmental hierarchy: phantasia as developmental gradient
readings.thesis: The three kinds of phantasia correlate not just with classes of animals but with a DEVELOPMENTAL gradient of cognitive sophistication: indefinite (lowest, in imperfectly developed creatures) → sensitive (middle, in all multi-sensed irrational animals) → calculative (highest, in rational humans). The article's title ('three kinds OR GRADES') signals the gradient interpretation.
readings.contestation: The 'grades' interpretation distinguishes Papachristou's reading from a purely TAXONOMIC three-types reading. It connects to Aristotle's broader scala naturae and to the threptike-aisthetike-noetike hierarchy of soul-powers from DA II.3. Has parallels with Nussbaum 1985's seeing-as-shared-with-animals account but pushes a stronger gradient: not just continuity between human and animal cognition, but a three-tier developmental staircase.

tensions.label: Three kinds vs. two kinds: revising the binary at DA III.10 433b29
tensions.description: Papachristou's central interpretive tension: DA III.10 433b29 ('all phantasia is either calculative or sensitive') has been read by most modern interpreters as a binary taxonomy. Papachristou argues this is incomplete — the imperfect-animals passage at DA III.11 433b31-434a5, together with Themistius, Philoponus, and Aquinas's commentaries, requires a THIRD, sub-sensitive tier of indefinite/indeterminate phantasia. The binary is not abandoned but recontextualized as a higher-level dichotomy within a tripartite scheme.

tensions.label: Animalia imperfecta really have phantasia, or only its 'traces'?
tensions.description: Aristotle at DA III.11 433b31-434a5 hesitates: how could imperfect animals have phantasia at all? They have it 'but indefinitely' (ἀορίστως). Papachristou (following Aquinas) reads them as genuinely possessing phantasia, but Aquinas himself notes that 'the motion of phantasy does not remain in them after the apprehension of the sense.' This raises a tension: is indefinite phantasia really phantasia in the full sense, or only its degenerate trace? Papachristou opts for 'really, but indeterminately' — but the conceptual cost is the very identity of phantasia across the tripartite scheme.

tensions.label: λογιστική vs. βουλευτική: equivalent epithets or substantive distinction?
tensions.description: Papachristou explicitly says λογιστική (calculative, DA III.10 433b29) and βουλευτική (deliberative, DA III.11 434a7) are EQUIVALENT, since 'λογίζομαι and βουλεύομαι both mean to determine, consider.' But the Aristotelian texts use them in different argumentative contexts. The tension is whether the equivalence is genuine or whether Aristotle's choice of διανύχν reflects different argumentative functions (theoretical reasoning vs. practical deliberation).

tensions.label: Ant-bee-scolex: textual emendation vs. textual integrity
tensions.description: Papachristou accepts Torstrik's emendation of DA III.3 428a10-11 to read 'ants and bees yes, scolex no.' This emendation is supported by Themistius and Sophonias and accepted by Hicks, Wallace, Ross. But the manuscript tradition includes the reading that denies phantasia to all three. The tension: should textual reconstruction be driven by philosophical considerations (consistency with Hist. Anim., De Part. Anim., Metaph., De Mem.) or by the principle of difficilior lectio?

tensions.label: Visual-imagery reading vs. wider Aristotelian functions of phantasia
tensions.description: Papachristou places great weight on πρὸ ὀμμάτων ποιήσασθαι at DA III.3 427b18-19 to identify phantasia primarily with VISUAL IMAGERY — 'seeing with the mind's eye.' But she also accepts Ross's list of six phantasia-functions (after-images, memory, recollection, dreams, desire-relation, thought-relation), most of which are not specifically visual. The tension is between the privileging of the visual register and the wider, multi-modal scope of Aristotelian phantasia.

tensions.label: Faculty-psychology language vs. unity of soul
tensions.description: Papachristou's six-fold Table 1 (nutritive/appetitive/sensitive/locomotive/imaginative/rational) is faculty-psychological in vocabulary; yet she insists that the parts/faculties of the soul 'form a unified whole.' The tension is between the analytical separation of faculties (μόρια, δυνάμεις) and Aristotle's emphasis on the unified hylomorphic soul. DA III.9 432a22-24 acknowledges that parts of the soul are 'in a sense innumerable' — an aporia Papachristou registers but does not resolve.

PHX-01-NUSSBAUM.evidence: fn. 34 (pdf p. 12): Nussbaum 1978 listed as one of the indicative readings on Aristotelian phantasia. Papachristou cites Nussbaum's 1978 first edition of De Motu Animalium ('The Role of Phantasia in Aristotle's Explanation of Action'), not the 1985 revision. No engagement with Nussbaum's substantive arguments in Papachristou's text.
PHX-01-NUSSBAUM.convergences: Both treat phantasia as critical for understanding animal action and the appetite-phantasia connection (DA III.10 433b28-29). Both engage the kath' hen formula at DA III.3 428a1-2.
PHX-01-NUSSBAUM.divergences: Nussbaum focuses on phantasia as 'seeing-as' supplying objects of desire (practical-motivational); Papachristou's tripartite scheme is taxonomic-developmental. Nussbaum does NOT distinguish indefinite from sensitive phantasia. Papachristou's Thomistic-Aquinas anchoring has no analogue in Nussbaum.

PHX-02-WHITE.evidence: fn. 34 (pdf p. 12): White 1985 listed as indicative reading on Aristotelian phantasia.
PHX-02-WHITE.convergences: Both share a Thomistic-scholastic disciplinary culture (Phillipe 1971, Roth 1963 background). Both invoke the kath' hen formula at DA III.3 428a1-2 as central. Both attend to the retention/persistence of phantasmata after sensation as a key Aristotelian doctrine.
PHX-02-WHITE.divergences: White restricts himself to DA III.3-8 and treats phantasia as preparation for noein; Papachristou expands across the corpus (DA I-III, Parva Naturalia, De Motu, Eth. Nic., Eth. Eud., Hist. Anim., De Part. Anim., De Gen. Anim., Metaph.) for the tripartite scheme. White makes no third-kind argument. White's interior-landscape culmination is Thomistic-humanist; Papachristou's culmination is taxonomic-cognitive (developmental-grade).

PHX-03-FREDE.evidence: fn. 34 (pdf p. 12): Frede 1992 listed as indicative reading.
PHX-03-FREDE.convergences: Both treat phantasia as supervenient on sensation (Aquinas's motus phantasiae remaining or not = Frede's supervenience criterion). Both accept the ant-bee inclusion under sensitive phantasia. Both find the retention of phantasmata cognitively important.
PHX-03-FREDE.divergences: Frede's supervenience account is analytic-philosophical and explicitly defends a binary (or unitary) phantasia; Papachristou's tripartite scheme requires Aquinas's distinction. Frede does not engage the Aquinas Latin tradition. Frede's account of indefinite-phantasia, where it appears, is closest to Papachristou's but not labeled as a separate kind.

PHX-04-CASTON.evidence: fn. 34 (pdf p. 12): Caston 1996 (Phronesis 41.1) listed as indicative reading.
PHX-04-CASTON.convergences: Both endorse the cognitive sophistication of irrational animals (ants, bees). Both treat DA III.3-11 as a unified discussion of phantasia.
PHX-04-CASTON.divergences: Caston defends a functionalist account of why Aristotle needs imagination (for representing the absent/non-existent); Papachristou's scheme is developmental-taxonomic. Caston does not deploy a tripartite division.

PHX-05-OGORMAN.evidence: O'Gorman 2005 not cited; Papachristou's bibliography does not include rhetorical-tradition phantasia scholarship.
PHX-05-OGORMAN.convergences: Both attend to phantasia's connection to visual imagery (πρὸ ὀμμάτων) and to its mnemonic and rhetorical uses (Simonides of Ceos).

PHX-06-GONZALEZ.evidence: Gonzalez 2006 not cited; Papachristou treats the De Anima phantasia, not the Rhetoric III.1 phantasia.

PHX-07-HAWHEE.evidence: Hawhee 2011 not cited; rhetorical-vision scholarship outside Papachristou's bibliography.

papachristou_distinctive_contributions: What Papachristou adds to the PHX cluster: (1) THE TRIPARTITE THESIS — the central, original interpretive claim that DA III contains THREE not two kinds of phantasia, anchored in Themistius, Philoponus, and especially Aquinas's Sentencia libri De anima Liber II. No prior PHX-01..07 unit (Nussbaum, White, Frede, Caston, O'Gorman, Gonzalez, Hawhee) develops this tripartite reading. (2) THE THOMISTIC-MEDIEVAL INTERLOCUTOR fully thematized — White 1985 has a Thomistic sensibility but does not name Aquinas; Papachristou explicitly cites Aquinas in Latin (fn. 57) and in English translation (fn. 67), grounding phantasia indeterminata + motus phantasiae + animalia imperfecta vs. perfecta as load-bearing technical terms. (3) THE FULL ZOOLOGICAL TAXONOMY — Table 4 systematically integrates Aristotle's blooded/bloodless (vertebrate/invertebrate) classification from Hist. Anim. and De Part. Anim. with the tripartite phantasia scheme; no other PHX unit reconstructs this zoological infrastructure. (4) THE TORSTRIK EMENDATION DEFENSE — sustained philological case for emending DA III.3 428a10-11 to credit ants and bees with phantasia (sensitive) but deny it to the scolex (first-stage larva, per Forbes 1930). (5) THE COGNITIVE-SCIENCE BRIDGE — Papachristou's fn. 94 connects Aristotle's pictorial-vs-propositional phantasmata to the Kosslyn-vs-Pylyshyn imagery debate, opening a contemporary cognitive-science bridge no other PHX unit ventures. (6) THE SIX-FOLD SOUL-POWER TABLE — Table 1's expansion of the canonical tripartite soul to a six-fold scheme (nutritive-reproductive, appetitive, sensitive, locomotive, imaginative, rational-with-passive-and-active-mind) systematizes a heuristic latent in Aristotle but not fully drawn out in PHX-01..07. (7) RECEPTION ARC — closing coda points forward to Stoic theory of phantasia (Papachristou's 2009 paper) and to Descartes' imagination, sketching a long-arc reception history that the cluster otherwise does not foreground.
